name: uri-percent-encoded-host-not-decoded-invalid
description: permittedSubtrees uniformResourceIdentifier is the host-form constraint 'example.com'. The leaf SAN encodes a URI whose authority host contains a percent-encoded letter that would decode to the same string: 'https://exam%70le.com/foo' (the '%70' is hex for the ASCII letter 'p'). RFC 3986 §3.2.2 defines the host as a reg-name production whose octet sequence is compared *as-is*: percent-encoded triplets within reg-name are reserved for non-ASCII octets in IRIs and are not unescaped during equality comparison. The constraint's literal 'example.com' therefore does not match the SAN's literal 'exam%70le.com'. Beyond simple non-equality, RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10 requires the URI constraint to be applied to the URI's host component — i.e. the *raw* reg-name text — so the chain must be rejected as outside the permitted subtree. Validators that normalise percent-encoded host octets before the constraint check (a defensible-sounding choice that violates RFC 3986 reg-name semantics) will incorrectly accept this leaf, which is the bypass vector an attacker would exploit to smuggle 'example.com'-shaped SANs past a constraint that intended to allow only the literal host.
notes: Bug bait is symmetric: a validator that percent-decodes the constraint side as well still arrives at the same string and would accept — but mainstream implementations don't percent-decode constraints, so the asymmetric SAN-side decoding is the realistic failure mode.
Distinct from `uri-host-hex-suffix-label-invalid`, which probes hex-shaped labels (no percent triplet); the bug here is reg-name decoding policy, not label syntax.
